summary:
Created by an 11-year-old using Google Sites, Machines of the Universe introduces three machines that made history in space exploration. The Opportunity rover found evidence that water once existed on Mars. The Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) helped Apollo astronauts travel farther across the Moon’s surface. Vanguard 1, one of Earth’s first artificial satellites, is still in orbit.

The project takes on the challenge “Machines of the Universe: Abandoned but not forgotten” by showing why these machines are worth remembering long after their missions ended. It invites visitors to discover why each machine was built, how it worked, and what it helped reveal about Mars, the Moon, and Earth.

For kids who are curious about the universe, the site brings science to life through questions they can ask themselves. How does a robot find clues about water in a rock? Why bring a car to the Moon? By exploring these stories in a project created by someone their own age, kids can imagine doing their own research, asking new questions, and sharing what they discover.
details:
Machines of the Universe is an educational website created by an 11-year-old. Visitors can explore the stories of three space machines: the Opportunity rover, the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), and the Vanguard 1 satellite. For each machine, the site invites visitors to discover why it was built, how it worked, and what its mission helped reveal. Presenting the machines as “retired” explorers ties the project together. A young astronaut invites visitors to explore their stories, and comic strips give the machines a voice. The theme Abandoned but not forgotten comes to life through characters that still have stories to tell about Mars, the Moon, and Earth.

The site helps kids understand how space machines solve real-world problems. When they learn about Opportunity, for example, they can discover how a robot studies rocks for clues about water on Mars. The stories of the three missions connect robotics, astronomy, and engineering to questions kids can ask on their own. The project aims to spark scientific curiosity and preserve the stories of machines that contributed to space exploration. Seeing a website created by someone their own age can also help kids imagine researching a topic they love and sharing what they learn.

The project was built and published using Google Sites, whose visual editor lets users organize pages, text, and images without writing code. This ease of use can encourage other kids to create their own websites to record their ideas, gather information, and share their interests. NASA was a source for research on the missions. The project’s design took into account the audience’s age, the clarity of the explanations, and the accuracy of the scientific information. Accessible language and visuals help explain the topics, while using the same three questions for each mission makes it easier to navigate the site and compare the machines.
